newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parliament to take up jobs bill in autumn.
newsitem.headline: French parliament to take up jobs bill in autumn.

text.p: A French government pledge to create 700,000 jobs for young people will be the top priority when parliament returns to work in mid-September, Parliamentary Relations Minister Daniel Vaillant said on Tuesday.

Vaillant told reporters parliament would be convened two weeks ahead of the usual beginning-of-October starting time due to the urgency of the jobs measure, a campaign promise of new leftist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.
"This is the most significant and the most urgent measure which is to be submitted to the Assembly upon its return," he said following a meeting of Jospin and Socialist deputies.

The meeting, convened a month after a leftist alliance of Socialists, Communists and Greens swept into power in France, was called to enable Jospin to outline the new government's priorities for his parliamentary allies.
Following the jobs measure, parliament will turn to a proposal reforming immigration law and citizenship and foreign residency requirements, Vaillant said.
Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has said he wants to restore the tradition of automatically granting citizenship to anyone born on French soil, which was dented by the previous conservative government.
The 1998 budget would be taken up by the National Assembly October 14-20, he added. A 1997 mini-budget, rejigging public finances for the current year, would also be taken up at this time, he said.
Jospin has ordered an audit of public finances, due in mid-July, before deciding whether a 1997 mini-budget will be needed.
The Maastricht Treaty requires European Union states to hold public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product during 1997 to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
But the new Jospin government has already acknowledged informally that France is not on track to meet the target.

Among other measures expected to be submitted to parliament before the end of the year are bills stiffening punishment of sex crimes, financing Social Security programmes in 1998, and banning the manufacture or export of land mines,

Measures to reduce the working week and limit the number of elective offices a public official can hold at one time will be taken up before the parliamentary session ends in late June 1998, Vaillant said.
Jospin pledged during the parliamentary campaign to limit the practice of multiple office-holding and to reduce the working week to 35 hours from 39, without a reduction in pay.

The prime minister said trimming working hours would make room for new workers and thus help combat France's record 12.8 percent unemployment. But he said the reductions would take place over five years.
